extracted.intended_audience: model aeroplane designers/builders and early aviators (hobbyists and experimenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical design, construction, and experimental guidelines for model aeroplanes and propellers, emphasizing aerodynamic form, materials selection, and building techniques for successful flight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller rotational velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: The velocity with which the propeller is rotated has an important bearing on efficiency; a higher speed than 900 r.p.m. does not appear desirable, and even 700 or less is generally preferable. In twin-screw propellers with tip angles 40°–45°, as low a velocity of 500 or even less would be still better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive r.p.m.; choose rotational speed appropriate to propeller geometry (lower speeds often preferable, especially for twin screws). (§15)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shrouding or tip rings
rubrics_metrics.description: No improvement whatever is obtained by the use of any kind of shrouding or ring round the propeller tips, or by corrugating the surface of the propeller, or by using cylindrical or cone-shaped propeller chamber or any kind of air guide either before or after the propeller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the propeller to revolve in as free an air-feed as possible; do not rely on tip-rings, shrouds, corrugations, or chambers to increase efficiency. (§16)

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller should act on a tube/cylinder of air
rubrics_metrics.description: The propeller should be so constructed as to act upon a tube and not a 'cylinder' (or tubes) of air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design blades and planform so the propeller drives a coherent column ('tube'/'cylinder') of air rather than disjointed tubes; avoid designs that break up the flow. (§17; echoed in experiment summary point 5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Blade planform shape
rubrics_metrics.description: A good shape for the blades is rectangular with rounded corners; the radius for rounding off the corners may be about one-quarter of the width of the blade. The width near the boss should be one-half the width at the tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a near-rectangular planform with rounded corners; scale boss/tip widths according to these proportions. (§18)

rubrics_metrics.name: Thickness and pitch distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The thickness should diminish uniformly from the boss to the tip. The pitch should be uniform and large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep blade thickness tapering toward the tip; maintain a consistent (and relatively large) pitch along the blade unless experimenting with variable pitch. (§18)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-blade, hollow-faced blades and concavity
rubrics_metrics.description: The blades, two in number and hollow faced — the maximum concavity being one-third the distance from the entering to the trailing edge; the ratio A T to O P (the width) being 0·048 or 1:21. The convex surface is as important as the concave, and the entire surface must have a true streamline form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design two hollow-faced blades with concavity up to one-third of the chord; ensure both concave and convex surfaces are streamlined. If entering/trailing edges are curved, make the straight edge the trailing edge; if both curved, the concave edge must be trailing. (§19)

rubrics_metrics.name: Blade leading/trailing-edge rule for curved edges
rubrics_metrics.description: If the entering and trailing edge be not both straight, but one be curved then the straight edge must be made the trailing edge; if both be curved then the concave edge must be the trailing edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When shaping curved blade edges, assign the straight or concave edge to be the trailing edge as specified to preserve flow characteristics. (§19, diagrams)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disc area ratio and blade area considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Blade area relates to disc area by a 'disc area ratio' (example: for a 14 in. diameter propeller area 10½ sq. in., yielding a disc-area-ratio ≈ 0·07).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing scale propellers compute disc area ratio to relate blade area to swept disc; use the geometric construction method given to lay out blade tip path and sections. (§19, Fig. 30–33)

rubrics_metrics.name: Boss diameter small relative to propeller
rubrics_metrics.description: In a propeller of 14 in. diameter the diameter of the 'boss' should not be more than 10/16 in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the hub/boss diameter small relative to the propeller diameter to maximise effective blade area. (§19 example)

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental apparatus and comparative testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Test propellers against one another under controlled conditions (e.g., parallel wires, swap props between wires, note times and distances, drive through smoke, attach silk threads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paired/comparative tests and swap setups to control for apparatus bias; observe dynamic thrust via motion through air, smoke, and lightweight indicators. (§20, Fig. 34–36)

rubrics_metrics.name: Static-thrust (fan-type) inefficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The inefficiency of a propeller of the fan blower or of the static thrust type is demonstrated by experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid static-blower style propellers for dynamic thrust applications; they may show early lead but fall off over distance. (experiment summary point 1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer hollow-faced blades and large diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantage of using propellers having hollow-faced blades and large diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a weight budget, favor hollow-faced blades and larger diameter (longer, thinner blades) over increased blade area. (experiment summary points 2 and 3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diameter more useful than blade area for a given weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Diameter was more useful than blade area, i.e., given a certain quantity (weight) of wood, make a long thin blade and not a shorter one of more blade area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate material to increase diameter and slenderness of blades rather than to increase chord/area when weight is limited. (experiment summary point 3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamline blade surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The propeller surface should be of true stream-line form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape both faces of blades into smooth streamline profiles to reduce losses and improve dynamic thrust. (experiment summary point 4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-size propeller scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: A correctly designed and proportioned propeller is just as efficacious in a small size of 9 in. to 28 in. as a full-sized propeller on a full-sized machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-proportioned small model propellers can match the performance characteristics of full-scale designs; scale geometry carefully. (experiment summary point 6)

rubrics_metrics.name: Best tip pitch angle
rubrics_metrics.description: The best angle of pitch (at the tip) was found to be from 20° to 30°.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tip pitch within ~20°–30° for good dynamic thrust; avoid excessive tip pitch. (experiments)

rubrics_metrics.name: Slip stream/back current necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: When the slip was as low as 25 per cent., or even somewhat less, nearly 20 per cent., a distinct 'back current' of air was given out by the screw. This 'slip stream' as it is caused, is absolutely necessary for efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow and expect slip-stream phenomena; designs should not eliminate slip entirely — a reasonable slip (e.g., ~20–25%) is part of efficient operation. (experiments)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabric-covered propellers: light but less efficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabric-covered screws did not give very efficient results; the only point in their use on model aeroplanes is their extreme lightness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fabric-covered propellers only where extreme lightness is required; wooden built-up propellers generally give better efficiency. (§21)

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin-screw configuration and blade curvature effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Twin screws turning in same direction can give good flights; curved-shaped propellers show superiority in dynamic thrust and can induce circling depending on placement. The double-curved blade is superior when made hollow-faced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with twin-screw layouts and blade curvature; be aware of torque and yaw effects — curved blades can produce directional tendencies and may be superior in thrust. (§22, Fig. 39)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extreme tip-pitch and excessive blade-area designs for efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Propellers with very large blade area and abnormal tip pitch (e.g., >45°) and large diameter do not necessarily give propeller efficiency or efficient dynamic thrust; tip-pitch over ~35° has not been found to give good dynamic thrust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long flights with limited turns (rubber motors), prefer larger diameter and moderate tip pitch (~25°) rather than extreme tip pitch; extreme pitch wastes energy in transverse upsetting torque. (§23)

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of pressure and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The resultant of upward sustaining forces acts at the 'Centre of Pressure.' Automatic stability depends on the movement of the centre of pressure when the angle of incidence varies; when the angle increases the centre of pressure moves backwards, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the aerofoil and planform so the centre of pressure moves in a stabilizing manner with changes in incidence; ensure longitudinal stability by managing CP movement relative to CG. (Ch. VI §1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of elevator/horizontal tail to damp oscillations
rubrics_metrics.description: The danger lies in 'oscillations' being set up due to changes in the position of the centre of pressure. Hence the device of an elevator or horizontal tail for the purpose of damping out such oscillations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a horizontal tail/elevator to dampen pitch oscillations caused by CP shifts and to assist restoring moments. (Ch. VI §2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Camber shape: aim for greatest lift with least drift
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem consists in ascertaining the most efficient aerocurve to give the greatest 'lift' with the least 'drift', and to investigate experimentally the movements of the centre of pressure at varying angles, and determine at what angle the 'reversal' takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select camber by experimentation on models; measure lift and CP travel to find optimal camber and critical reversal angle. (Ch. VI §3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dipping leading edge and small incidence angles
rubrics_metrics.description: The leading or front edge is not tangential to the line of flight but to a relative upward wind — a 'dipping front edge.' If a scientific treatment is desired the underside of the front edge can be given a negative angle of 5° to 7° for about one-eighth of the section length, thereafter a positive angle gradually increasing to about 4° at the trailing edge. But if any angle is used it should be a very small one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a small 'dipping' at the leading edge to meet the relative wind tangentially; overall angles of incidence should be very small in models. (Ch. VI §6)

rubrics_metrics.name: Camber depth location and magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest depth of the camber should be at one-third of the length of the section from the front edge, and the total depth measured from the top surface to the chord at this point should not be more than one-seventeenth of the length of section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make camber shallow: max depth at ~1/3 chord and about 1/17 of chord length. (Ch. VI §7)

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep camber very slight to avoid instability and drag
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the greatest mistake in model aeroplanes to make the camber otherwise than very slight (in the case of surfaced aerofoils the resistance is much increased), and aerofoils with anything but a very slight arch are liable to be very unstable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor very slight camber to minimise resistance and avoid instability; avoid strongly arched aerofoils on models. (Ch. VI §8)

rubrics_metrics.name: High aspect ratio for efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspect ratio (span/chord): the higher the aspect ratio the greater should be the efficiency. In models aspect ratio may with advantage be given a higher value than in full-sized machines. An aspect ratio of 10:1 or even 12:1 should be used if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design wings with high span/chord ratios where construction/strength permit; high aspect ratio reduces spanwise losses and limits CP travel. (Ch. VI §9)

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant vs varying camber — prefer slight and possibly flattened tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Some makers vary camber across the span; the writer's experiments incline towards further flattening of the camber in the end portions of the aerofoil. In all cases camber should be very slight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If varying camber, consider flattening towards the tips; ensure overall camber remains slight. (Ch. VI §10)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of centre-of-pressure reversal critical angle
rubrics_metrics.description: On arched surfaces the centre of pressure moves forward until a certain critical angle of incidence is reached, after which a reversal takes place and the centre of pressure moves backwards. Experiments place this critical angle between about 16° and 20° (Sellers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep operational incidence angles well below the critical reversal angle used in models; further experiments recommended to locate exact reversal for a given aerofoil. (Ch. VI §3, §11)

rubrics_metrics.name: Material selection: lightness, strength, elasticity, and resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of materials is limited: lightness relative to strength, great elasticity, and especially great resilience (capacity to absorb shock without injury) are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select materials that balance weight, strength, elasticity and resilience for best model performance. (Ch. VII §1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Bamboo use and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Bamboo has per pound weight a greater resilience than any other suitable substance; use for struts, spars, ribs, and long struts supporting the rubber motor. Bamboo may be bent by dry heat or preferably steaming; when bent it should be bound on a former and left to dry. Bamboo tends to split at ends; joints require care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bamboo tubing where resilience-to-weight ratio is important; steam-bend and bind to form shapes; guard against splitting and use appropriate jointing (lashing to light metal strips). (Ch. VII §2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Wood selection and seasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Ash, spruce, whitewood, poplar etc. are used; wood of same kind can differ in strength. For model aeroplanes all wood used should have been at least a year in seasoning and should be treated so it cannot absorb moisture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose woods for strength-to-weight and resilience; season wood ≥1 year and protect from moisture; consider relative resilience values when selecting species. (Ch. VII §3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Steel tubing and umbrella steel considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Steel has much higher transverse rupture but is far heavier. Steel tubing of sufficiently small bore was not widely available; umbrella-section steel (specific sizes given) can be used successfully for aerofoil front and ends and joined for longer lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider steel (including umbrella-section) for places needing small cross-section strength; account for its greater density and potential drag from larger bulk if used in place of timber. (Ch. VII §4–5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Steel wire for stays and tension members
rubrics_metrics.description: Steel wire tensile strength about 300,000 lb. per sq. in. For aerofoil framework of small models and for stays and where a strong and light tension is required, steel wire is invaluable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use steel wire for stays, spars when in tension, skids, shock absorbers, and hooks for rubber motors. (Ch. VII §6)

rubrics_metrics.name: Silk as covering material
rubrics_metrics.description: Silk is the strongest organic substance for certain parts of construction and for aerofoil surface no substance can compare with it, but it must be used in the form of oiled or specially treated silk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use oiled/specially treated silk fabrics (e.g., Hart's 'fabric') to cover aerofoils for high strength-to-weight. (Ch. VII §7)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alloys and aluminium caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Aluminium and magnalium are not recommended except for fittings or scale models; steel is generally preferable weight for weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on light alloys for structural flying parts unless exceptional circumstances (very light in-wind flyers); prefer steel for overall performance. (Ch. VII §8–9)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use or avoidance of miscellaneous sheet materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheet ebonite, vulcanized fibre, and sheet celluloid can be useful for small propellers; celluloid becomes brittle and shrinks; mica should be avoided. Jointless cane, three/four/five-ply wood, hollow reeds and porcupine quills may have useful roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select these materials for experimental or specific lightweight components but be wary of long-term degradation (e.g., celluloid). (Ch. VII §10)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interrupting continuity of structural members
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not interrupt the continuity of any rib, tube, spar, etc., by drilling holes or making too thinned down holding places; if done, additional strength by binding (with thread, not wire), or by slipping a small piece of slightly larger tube over the other, must be imparted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain continuous members where possible; where weakened do reinforcement by lashing with thread or sleeve joints rather than drilling/thinning. (Ch. VIII §2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with simple monoplane
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by making a simple monoplane, and afterwards as you gain skill and experience proceed to more elaborate and scientific models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progressively build skills: start simple before attempting complex designs. (Ch. VIII §3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to solder
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn to solder—it is absolutely essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquire soldering skill as a basic workshop technique for model construction. (Ch. VIII §4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tractor screw-main plane front with tail behind in models
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not construct models (intended for actual flight) with a tractor screw-main plane in front and tail (behind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises against building models with a tractor (tractor-prop) main plane in front and tail behind for actual flight; prefer other arrangements (implicit preference for different configuration). (Ch. VIII §5)
